issues.legal_issue: A summary administrative inquiry into trust mismanagement does not exclude civil-court jurisdiction over serious allegations of fraud or forgery requiring determination on evidence.
material_facts: The suit concerned the management and property of a charitable trust and alleged forgery, fraud, and diversion of trust property.
The administrative inquiry contemplated by the governing law was a summary inquiry conducted in the manner of a formal revenue inquiry.
The claims required issues to be framed and determined on evidence.
issues.conclusion: The summary inquiry provisions did not bar the civil court from hearing the serious allegations in the suit; those matters required determination by a court on evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17, 18, 37 and 40 of the Mysore Religious and Charitable Institutions Act, 1927, the Muzrai Officer could conduct a summary inquiry into gross mismanagement and make the specified orders, with prior government sanction for an order under Section 18. Section 18(5) authorizes only ancillary or necessary orders relating to the matters in sub-sections (1) to (4); it does not empower the Officer to adjudicate serious fraud or forgery allegations. Summary inquiries of this kind do not bar civil-court jurisdiction over matters requiring judicial determination.

predicates.public_trust_administration_suit: A civil suit concerns the administration or property of a public charitable or religious trust.
predicates.serious_fraud_or_forgery_allegations: The suit alleges serious fraud or forgery relating to the trust or its property.
predicates.summary_agency_inquiry_cannot_determine_: The available agency inquiry is summary and cannot determine the claims through the evidentiary process required for their resolution.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerns trust administration, raises serious fraud or forgery allegations, and those claims cannot be resolved in a summary agency inquiry, a civil court may determine them.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on civil-court jurisdiction does not defeat a public-trust suit where the governing enactment preserves that suit despite agency orders and an amendment makes the enactment’s reference to an earlier procedural code refer to its replacement.
material_facts: The suit was brought under the civil-procedure provision for suits concerning public trusts.
The governing enactment stated that an order made under it would not bar such a suit.

The enactment referred to the civil-procedure code applicable when it was passed; a later amendment made the replacement code applicable throughout India and provided that references to repealed laws should, where practicable, be read as references to corresponding provisions of the replacement code.
issues.conclusion: The suit under the public-trust provision was not barred, whether or not an agency order had been made; the enactment’s reference to the earlier code applied to the corresponding provision of the replacement code.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40A of the Mysore Religious and Charitable Institutions Act, 1927, provides that an order under that Act does not bar a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1911. Section 20(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1951 provides that, so far as practicable, references in existing laws to repealed laws are to be taken as references to the corresponding provisions of the replacement Code. The Court held that the reference therefore meant Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and that the suit was not barred even where no agency order had been made.

predicates.public_trust_provision_suit: A suit is brought under the civil-procedure provision allowing suits concerning public trusts.
predicates.preservation_clause_allows_suit_despite_: The governing enactment provides that an agency order does not bar a suit of this kind.
predicates.procedural_amendment_maps_old_code_refer: A procedural amendment directs that references to a repealed code be read, where practicable, as references to corresponding provisions of its replacement.

issues.definition: If a public-trust suit is covered by a clause preserving it despite agency orders and a procedural amendment maps the old-code reference to the replacement code, the suit is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: A party that opposed leave to bring a public-trust suit and lost cannot subsequently seek rejection of the plaint after leave has been granted.
material_facts: Leave to bring the suit was granted after the parties had been heard.
The appellants had opposed the grant of leave and their opposition was unsuccessful.
After leave was granted, the appellants applied for rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent application to reject the plaint was not open to the appellants; it should have been made before leave was granted or when they opposed leave.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, once leave to bring the suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been granted after hearing the parties, rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 did not arise. A party that had already opposed leave could not, after losing that opposition, make a later application for rejection of the plaint.

rule.if: public_trust_suit and leave_granted_after_hearing and applicant_opposed_leave_and_lost and rejection_application_made_after_leave

predicates.public_trust_suit: The proceeding is a suit brought under the civil-procedure provision for suits concerning public trusts.
predicates.leave_granted_after_hearing: The court granted permission to bring the suit after hearing the parties.
predicates.applicant_opposed_leave_and_lost: The applicant opposed permission to bring the suit and the court rejected that opposition.
predicates.rejection_application_made_after_leave: The applicant sought rejection of the plaint only after permission had been granted.

issues.definition: When a party unsuccessfully opposes leave in a public-trust suit and seeks rejection of the plaint only after leave is granted, that later application is not open.

issues.legal_issue: The procedural law and jurisdiction applicable when a pending suit comes on for trial or disposal govern, rather than the procedural law in force when the suit was instituted.
material_facts: The suit was instituted while the relevant state enactment was in force.
That enactment was later repealed before the court considered whether the suit could proceed.
At the time of consideration, the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit, and the court that would receive a returned plaint was the same court.
issues.conclusion: The jurisdiction question was to be determined under the law in force when the suit came on for trial or disposal; the court could not refuse jurisdiction solely because the law was different when the suit was instituted.
issues.legal_principle: Procedural laws apply retrospectively unless the legislature states otherwise, and no party has a vested right to a particular procedure or forum. The Court adopted the reasoning in Shiv Bhagwan v. Onkarmal, AIR 1952 Bombay 365: the court must apply the procedural law in force when the proceeding comes on for trial or disposal and take account of intervening changes in law.

predicates.civil_suit_pending: A civil suit remains pending for trial or disposal.
predicates.procedural_forum_law_changed_before_tria: The law governing procedure or forum changes after the suit is instituted but before trial or disposal.
predicates.current_court_has_jurisdiction: The court has jurisdiction to hear the suit under the law in force when the suit comes on for trial or disposal.

issues.definition: For a pending civil suit, if the procedural or forum law changes before trial or disposal and the court then has jurisdiction, jurisdiction is determined under the law then in force.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal concerning the management and property of a trust cannot proceed after the trust, which is a necessary party, is removed from the appeal.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the management of a trust and its property.
The trust was a necessary party to the appeal.
At the appellants’ request, the trust was deleted from the array of parties in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was required to be dismissed because the appellants had removed a necessary party to the dispute.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the trust whose management and property were in dispute was not merely a proper party but a necessary party; its removal from the appeal furnished an independent reason to dismiss the appeal.

predicates.appeal_concerns_trust_management_or_prop: The appeal concerns the management or property of a trust.
predicates.trust_is_necessary_party: The trust is a necessary party to resolve the dispute in the appeal.
predicates.appellant_removes_trust_from_appeal: The appellant causes the trust to be removed from the parties to the appeal.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns trust management or property, the trust is a necessary party, and the appellant removes it, the appeal is dismissed for absence of a necessary party.
